headline: Approved solar canopy purchase at 585 Pine Street and adopted 2026-2027 Strategic Direction, 5-0 each
summary: The commission heard public comments on carbon capture and wood pyrolysis technologies, reviewed FY26 and FY27 financial results, and discussed the status of the PUC business process audit. After an executive session, the commission approved a capital purchase of a solar parking canopy for 585 Pine Street and approved the 2026-2027 Strategic Direction document.
decisions: Accepted the July 8, 2026 minutes as presented, 5-0.
Found that premature public knowledge of solar canopy contract negotiations would disadvantage the Commission, 5-0.
Entered executive session to discuss solar canopy contract negotiations, 5-0.
Approved BED's capital purchase of a solar parking canopy for 585 Pine Street, funded from available bond proceeds, 5-0.
Approved the 2026-2027 Strategic Direction as presented, 5-0.

decision_evidence.quote: Commissioner Dawson moved to accept the July 8, 2026 minutes as presented; Commissioner Vota seconded the motion. Vote: 5 ayes 0 nays.

Commissioner Vota made a motion that the Commission find that premature general public knowledge of contract negotiations related to the Commission and BED's negotiating position and strategy for a proposed solar canopy, to be located at 585 Pine Street, would clearly place the Commission and BED at a substantial disadvantage in those negotiations. Commissioner Bonn seconded the motion. Vote: 5 ayes 0 nays.

Commissioner Bonn made a motion that the Commission enter executive session, with BED staff present, pursuant to 1 V.S.A. § 313(a)(1)(A) to discuss ongoing contract negotiations regarding a proposed solar canopy to be located at 585 Pine Street. Commissioner Dawson seconded the motion. Vote: 5 ayes 0 nays.
Commissioner Vota made a motion to exit executive session; Commissioner Dawson seconded. Vote: 5 ayes 0 nays.

Commissioner Bonn made a motion that the Commission approve BED's capital purchase of a solar parking canopy for 585 Pine Street, to be funded from available bond proceeds, as presented at tonight's meeting. Commissioner Vota seconded the motion. Vote: 5 ayes 0 nays.
Commissioner Vota made a motion that the commission approve the 2026-2027 Strategic Direction as presented at tonight's meeting. Commissioner Dawson seconded the motion. Vote: 5 aye 0 nay.

1 
 
 
 
DRAFT 
MINUTES OF REGULAR MEETING 
BURLINGTON ELECTRIC COMMISSION 
 
Wednesday, September 9, 2026 
                  
The regular meeting of the Burlington Electric Commission was convened at 5:03 p.m. on 
Wednesday, September 9, 2026, at Burlington Electric Department, 585 Pine Street, Burlington, 
Vermont, and on Microsoft Teams. 
 
Attendance 
 Channel 17 was present to record this meeting. 
 Commissioners Lara Bonn, Paul Dawson, Ali Kenney, and Andy Vota were present at 585 
Pine Street.  
 Commissioner Brian Williams was present via Microsoft Teams.  
 Staff members Paul Alexander, Dan Edson, Mike Kanarick, Munir Kasti, Katie Morris, Darren 
Springer, and Emily Stebbins-Wheelock were present at 585 Pine Street. 
 Staff members Seth Clifford and James Gibbons was present via Microsoft Teams.  
 Public members Leendert Huisman and Peter Macausland were present at 585 Pine Street. 
 Public member Pike Porter was present via Microsoft Teams.  
 
1. Agenda 
There were no changes to the agenda.  
 
2. Meeting Minutes 
Commissioner Dawson moved to accept the July 8, 2026 minutes as presented; Commissioner Vota 
seconded the motion. Vote: 5 ayes 0 nays.  
 
3. Public Forum 
Leendert Huisman addressed the commission regarding the Valerity report. Mr. Huisman 
welcomed what he characterized as BED's acknowledgment that McNeil emits significant 
greenhouse gases, and expressed hope that BED no longer treats wood-burning emissions as 
climate-neutral on the theory that they are offset by forest regrowth. Mr. Huisman asked whether 
carbon capture remains under consideration as an action item from the Valerity Report, alongside 
pyrolysis. 
 
General Manager Darren Springer clarified he did not agree with Huisman's characterization of 
BED's position. Following the Valerity Report, BED issued a Request for Information (RFI) in 
December 2025 covering three technologies highlighted in the report: organic Rankine cycle 
turbines, carbon capture, and wood pyrolysis.
2 
 
 
 
One proposal was received for organic Rankine cycle technology, but it did not benefit BED at its 
operating scale. One proposal was received for wood pyrolysis; BED has since issued an RFP for a 
demonstration unit (up to 2.2 MW) at the facility. No proposals were received for carbon capture, 
and BED is not currently pursuing work in that area. 
 
Mr. Huisman noted he has not yet studied pyrolysis in depth but hopes to comment on it next 
month. The core objection to carbon capture is that it converts gaseous CO2 to liquid form but does 
not reduce the total amount of CO2 produced. Liquid CO2 has commercial but eventually 
evaporates back into the atmosphere. From a global perspective Mr. Huisman believes this results 
in no net change. The CO2 from burning wood is still ultimately vented; it only shifts accounting 
responsibility from BED's books to another party's. Mr. Huisman raised the question of whether 
this outcome aligns with the intent of the Burlington City Council's request for greenhouse gas 
reductions from McNeil and urged the commission to consider this distinction carefully when 
evaluating carbon capture as a strategy. 
 
Peter Macausland addressed the commission and raised a concern about whether pyrolysis 
technology, based on the ongoing Lyndonville case, will meet the state's required 60% efficiency 
standard, and noted the Lyndonville case has been in progress for two years. Mr. Macausland 
suggested BED should consider using that case as a benchmark rather than conducting its own 
separate testing, while acknowledging BED's preference to run its own evaluation. Mr. Macausland 
also raised a second concern regarding wood supply sourced from Bennington County, questioning 
whether this would adversely impact BED's current relationships or agreements with existing 
wood chip suppliers. 
 
4. Monthly Impact Minute 
Dan Edson is BED’s new Manager of Energy Services, noting he has been in the role for 
approximately two months. He highlighted the BED team's dedication to the community as the most 
impactful part of his experience so far. Mr. Edson reported renewed engagement from UVM and the 
hospital over the past month (and generally over the past two months) regarding energy efficiency 
programs. Both institutions have shown renewed enthusiasm for communicating with BED and 
investing their own funding in facility efficiency improvements. These include the installation of 
hybrid heat pump RTUs (rooftop units) at the Miller Center, with the facility being positioned as the 
city's first net-zero facility, relying primarily on electricity for heating needs. The units do use some 
natural gas, but this will be offset through the purchase of renewable natural gas credits from 
Vermont Gas. 
 
Commissioner Dawson asked what drove UVM's renewed interest. 
 
Mr. Edson attributed the change primarily to personnel. UVM's "energy champion" had been on 
parental leave and has since returned. This employee is responsible for developing efficiency
3 
 
 
 
project proposals and securing funding through UVM's revolving fund. With his return, the proposal 
and funding process is active again. Mr. Edson noted personal familiarity with this type of process 
from his prior role as State Energy Manager and expressed enthusiasm about collaborating with 
UVM's team. 
 
5. Commissioners’ Corner 
There were no topics discussed.  
 
6. GM Update 
General Manager Darren Springer welcomed Dan Edson, noting his background at Efficiency 
Vermont and with the state, and praised his work leading the energy services team. 
 
The 5th annual Net Zero Festival was held August 22, 2026 at the waterfront (a new location), 
drawing higher attendance than in past years at 585 Pine Street, based on anecdotal reports. 
It featured live induction cooking demos, including a battery-powered induction stove (plugs into a 
standard outlet) and a Bouchard Pierce induction stove (240V outlet). The weather cooperated for 
the outdoor event; BED plans to meet soon to gather ideas for improving next year's festival. 
 
BED will bring a solar canopy proposal forward later in the meeting, following completion of an 
RFP process, and a PowerPoint presentation will follow. 
 
The RFP for a wood pyrolysis demonstration unit (up to 2.2 MW) closes September 30, 2026 and is 
posted on BED's website. This stems from the Valerity report and prior RFI process. The goal is to 
assess viability of installing the unit at McNeil, evaluate efficiency and environmental benefits, and 
build internal familiarity with the technology. Referencing Peter Macausland's earlier public 
comment about the Lyndonville project, Mr. Springer confirmed a 2.2 MW pyrolysis project is 
planned for Lyndonville but is not yet operational. BED may learn from that project, but direct, on-
site experience at McNeil is considered valuable in its own right. 
 
BED intends to pursue a PPA (not direct purchase) so financing, permitting, and construction risk 
sit with the vendor; BED would have an option to buy later. This differs from the solar canopy 
project, which BED intends to purchase and own/maintain directly, and is positioned alongside the 
McNeil battery storage project and solar canopy as part of BED's push to advance tangible 
renewable energy infrastructure. 
 
BED's 2.99% rate case has been approved by the PUC. The under-3% rate change avoided a 
litigated process, which is typically 7+ months, supporting both affordability and staff efficiency. 
Customers will see the rate change reflected on bills starting in October — notably faster than the 
usual surcharge-then-rate-change pattern.
4 
 
 
 
Commissioner Vota asked about the status of the business process audit: 
 
Mr. Springer responded that it remains an open, litigated docket at the PUC. The audit report was 
issued July 31, 2026; BED and the Department of Public Service did not pursue discovery, 
evidentiary hearings, or additional testimony, and BED intends to implement the report's 
recommendations pending a PUC order. Pre-filed testimony is due by the end of the week, and is 
expected to reiterate BED's support for the recommendations without caveat. Mr. Springer noted 
limits on what he could share given the litigated status but offered an executive session if the 
commission wants more detail. BED hopes to have ARC (the audit firm/entity) join a future 
commission meeting to discuss the report once the PUC process concludes. 
 
Commissioner Kenney requested ongoing updates on PUC progress. Mr. Springer agreed to 
continue to provide updates. 
 
Mr. Springer noted the strategic direction update will occur later in the meeting and will include a 
specific item on implementing the audit recommendations, calling it a top priority. 
 
Commissioner Kenney asked for clarification on implementation timing. 
 
Mr. Springer responded that some actions can begin now, but the formal implementation roadmap 
and milestone clock are tied to the date of a PUC order requiring implementation. 
 
7. Financials: Preliminary June FY26 
Emily Stebbins-Wheelock, CFO and Manager of Strategy and Innovation, presented the preliminary 
unaudited June FY26 financial results.  
 
One additional post-closing adjustment is still expected, related to OPEB (other post-employment 
benefit) liability, pending information from the city's actuaries; not typically material. The full 
audited financials will be presented by Amanda Hurlbut, Controller, at the November commission 
meeting. 
 
Actual net income was approximately $3 million vs. a budgeted $2.2 million — a positive result 
overall. However, operating revenues came in $868,000 under budget; operating expenses were 
roughly on budget but not enough under budget to offset the revenue shortfall. REC (renewable 
energy credit) revenue was identified as a major drag on the adjusted debt service coverage ratio 
(ADSCR). Positive net income was primarily driven by a $1.5 million favorable variance in ‘other 
income and deductions,’ mainly from:  
 Timing of the final FEMA grant reimbursement for the rubber dam replacement. 
 Earlier billing (but FY26 receipt) of customer contributions from the city for the Champlain 
Parkway and Main Street projects.
5 
 
 
 
The debt service coverage ratio (ADSCR) was significantly weaker than budget, driven by weak 
operating revenues and higher-than-budgeted interest expense. The most recent 12-month ADSCR 
was 1.03, vs. a budgeted target of 1.15. The three-year average ADSCR was 1.32, which is the metric 
used on the Moody's scorecard and considered healthy; this average is designed to absorb a single 
bad year, but consecutive weak years would be a concern. 
 
Total capital spending landed just under $9 million, in line with May projections. Generation spent 
about 75% of its budget. Distribution, IT, and facilities collectively spent about 50%, with 
distribution comprising the majority of the capital budget. 
 
June ended with $14.7 million in operating cash; $1.5 million better than budget and 147 days cash 
on hand (including line of credit) / 90 (excluding line of credit).  
 
Commissioner Bonn asked about next steps for the debt service coverage ratio. 
 
Ms. Stebbins-Wheelock noted the 3-year average (1.32) remains healthy but reiterated the goal of 
returning to range in FY27. 
 
Commissioner Kenney asked what steps will be taken to achieve that goal.  
 
Ms. Stebbins-Wheelock responded that the standard process is to monitor monthly results and 
reforecast expected year-end position. 
 
FY26 controllable actions included O&M spending cuts and directors giving back budget to 
minimize OPEX, though there are limits to this lever. Uncontrollable factors included sales revenue 
(a positive factor this year, driven by usage and customer growth, largely outside BED's control 
except via rate increases) and REC revenues (dependent on renewable generation output, i.e., wind 
and river conditions). BED is working to maximize output from dispatchable resources (gas turbine, 
McNeil) since most of the power supply revenue shortfall stems from lower-than-expected 
production, not REC pricing. Weather alone can swing sales revenue by $1–2 million. 
 
Commissioner Williams asked why net income exceeded budget while the ratio declined. 
 
Ms. Stebbins-Wheelock responded that ADSCR reflects operating income/excess revenue available 
to cover debt service. The favorable "other income and deductions" variance boosted net income 
but is mostly non-recurring, so it doesn't count toward the operating revenue used in the ADSCR 
calculation. 
 
Commissioner Dawson asked about the budgeted $1.2 million operating loss.
6 
 
 
 
Ms. Stebbins-Wheelock noted this is not unusual for BED; budgeting an operating loss is acceptable 
as long as cash projections and coverage ratios remain within target. 
 
Darren Springer clarified that dividend revenue from BED's ownership shares in VELCO appears in 
"other income and deductions," not operating income, so it doesn't help the ADSCR. However, 
transmission expense (which these dividends are meant to partially offset) is recorded in operating 
expense, creating a structural disconnect. This explains why operating income can be negative even 
with several million dollars in dividend income. 
 
Commissioner Dawson asked about variance in capital budget spending percentages. 
 
Ms. Stebbins-Wheelock responded that they are not financially driven; explanations include:  
 IT/general line: delays in software implementation projects (project management delays, 
later-than-expected kickoffs). 
 Distribution line: delays due to transformers on order but not yet delivered (supply chain 
lead times), accounting for roughly $750,000 of the variance. 
 Two grant-funded projects couldn't begin until grant agreements were signed (finalized 
June 30), pushing work into FY27. 
 Capital contingency/set-aside funds for storm/outage-related repairs were largely unused 
in FY26 due to fewer major incidents. 
 
Commissioner Kenney asked how FY26 delays affect FY27 budgeting. 
 
Ms. Stebbins-Wheelock responded that some delayed projects carried over into FY27 with 
associated spending, even though they were originally FY26-budgeted. 
 Outage-related capital contingency funds are budgeted again for FY27. 
 IT project milestones and payment schedules have been revised for the FY27 budget. 
 
Amanda Hurlbut, Controller, will present the full audited FY26 financials at the November 
commission meeting. BED will continue monthly monitoring and reforecasting to improve ADSCR 
performance in FY27 and continue efforts to maximize dispatchable generation to support power 
supply revenu 
 
8. Financials: July FY27 
Emily Stebbins-Wheelock, CFO and Manager of Strategy & Innovation, presented July 2026 ϐinancial 
results. 
 
July is the ϐirst month of the ϐiscal year, so monthly and year-to-date ϐigures match. There was a 
budgeted net income of $96,000 vs. actual net income of $2.2 million. The primary driver was REC
7 
 
 
 
deliveries. Most RECs budgeted for August delivery were instead delivered in July, pulling revenue 
forward. Some additional REC revenue will be booked in August. 
 
Year-to-date power supply revenue is expected to be on budget once August results are ϐinalized; a 
positive sign for the ϐirst quarter. Net power supply expense was slightly below budget ($110,000 
variance). Operating expense was slightly over budget. Payment in lieu of taxes and Winooski 
property taxes were slightly under budget with small variances expected in this line throughout the 
year. 
 
Capital spending was budgeted at $1.2 million for July; actual spend was $600,000 spread fairly 
evenly across generation, distribution, and general plant (about 6% of the total annual capital 
budget). 
 
Cash position was $16.4 million vs. $14 million budgeted; $2.5 million favorable. Days cash on hand 
were 154. The ADSCR was 1.28, boosted by strong REC revenue improving operating income. 
 
Commissioner Dawson asked about drivers behind customer sales trends. 
 
Ms. Stebbins-Wheelock noted average temperatures were close to budgeted expectations, but 
cooling degree days came in lower than budgeted (heating degree days were roughly as expected), 
which likely explains softer-than-budgeted sales. 
 
Commissioner Williams noted that cooling degree days have been unusually low in August and into 
September, raising concern that this trend could continue to suppress revenue. 
 
Commissioner Kenney asked why power supply costs were over budget, and whether McNeil's 
underperformance was a factor . 
 
Ms. Stebbins-Wheelock explained that BED's three wind projects produced more than budgeted this 
month. McNeil produced less, reducing fuel costs but shifting BED's ISO exchange position from long 
(as budgeted) to short, contributing to the unfavorable variance. A new long-term contract 
(Brookϐield Hydro) was signed after the budget was set using a placeholder estimate, creating an 
ongoing variance against the modeled ϐigure. 
 
James Gibbons, Director of Policy and Planning, commented that BED has had to purchase 
replacement power due to underperformance at McNeil. Hydro resources broadly are performing 
poorly across the region this year, and replacement power is currently expensive. Wood and 
biomass resources are underperforming; wind performed well this month.
8 
 
 
 
Ms. Stebbins-Wheelock added that McNeil's issues stemmed primarily from tube leaks and backed-
up ash grates, which caused unexpected outages requiring repair. 
 
Commissioner Vota asked about an unusual spike in arrearages in July that declined signiϐicantly by 
August, per the strategic direction dashboard.  
 
Ms. Stebbins-Wheelock explained that a large customer experienced administrative system changes 
that caused them to miss bills or be unable to pay through normal channels, falling several months 
behind. The customer has since caught up and resolved the balance. The over-60-day balance 
(currently $512,000) is now at its lowest level since March 2025.  
 
9. Solar Canopy Executive Session 
General Manager Darren Springer and James Gibbons, Director of Policy and Planning, presented 
information about a proposed solar canopy project at 585 Pine Street.  
 
Project overview: 
 Proposal for a timber frame solar canopy covering the customer and visitor parking area in 
front of BED's facility. 
 System size: approximately 130 kW. 
 Will use bifacial panels, which also generate from reflected light (e.g., off snow) on the 
underside, boosting winter production. 
 Structured as a direct capital purchase (owned and maintained by BED), different from the 
PPA structure used for the wood pyrolysis project. 
 Supports BED's broader in-city solar and "lead by example" initiatives. 
 Expected annual production: approximately 136 MWh. 
 
RFP evaluation criteria (developed with contributions from James Gibbons and the policy and 
planning team): 
 Pricing, capacity, and generation output. 
 Panel type (bifacial preferred). 
 Production guarantees and degradation rates over time. 
 O&M costs, project life, and manufacturer warranties (inverters, panels, and timber frame 
structure). 
 Minimal soil disturbance, given the site's Superfund status. 
 Preservation of customer parking and winter plowing operations. 
 Vendor experience with similar projects. 
 
Tax credit considerations: 
 Base Investment Tax Credit (ITC): 30%.
9 
 
 
 
 Originally stemming from the Inflation Reduction Act, but modified by legislation passed 
last summer, resulting in a faster phase-out timeline than originally planned. Construction 
must be completed by the end of next year to qualify. 
 Potential additional 10% bonus credit for brownfield sites — BED believes its Superfund 
site likely qualifies and plans to confirm this. 
 Potential additional credit for domestic content (threshold currently 50%, possibly rising to 
55% next year). 
 
Further detailed discussion of the proposal is planned for executive session, with public session to 
follow. 
 
Commissioner Vota made a motion that the Commission find that premature general public 
knowledge of contract negotiations related to the Commission and BED’s negotiating position and 
strategy for a proposed solar canopy, to be located at 585 Pine Street, would clearly place the 
Commission and BED at a substantial disadvantage in those negotiations. Commissioner Bonn 
seconded the motion. Vote: 5 ayes 0 nays. 
 
Based on that finding, Commissioner Bonn made a motion that the Commission enter executive 
session, with BED staff present, pursuant to 1 V.S.A. § 313(a)(1)(A) to discuss ongoing contract 
negotiations regarding a proposed solar canopy to be located at 585 Pine Street. Commissioner 
Dawson seconded the motion. Vote: 5 ayes 0 nays. The Burlington Electric commission entered 
executive session at 5:59 p.m. 
 
Commissioner Vota made a motion to exit executive session; Commissioner Dawson seconded. 
Vote: 5 ayes 0 nays. The Burlington Electric commission exited executive session at 6:33 p.m.  
 
10. Solar Canopy Discussion & Vote 
Commissioner Bonn made a motion that the Commission approve BED’s capital purchase of a solar 
parking canopy for 585 Pine Street, to be funded from available bond proceeds, as presented at 
tonight’s meeting. Commissioner Vota seconded the motion. Vote: 5 ayes 0 nays.  
 
11. 2026-2027 Strategic Direction 
Commissioner Kenney noted that the vote on the Strategic Direction was deferred from the July 8th 
meeting to allow time to incorporate commission feedback on things such as energy supply 
resource strategy, McNeil's role, dashboard metrics. 
 
General Manager Darren Springer presented changes to the proposed 2026-2027 strategic 
direction: 
 The document was reformatted for improved clarity and organization following further 
discussion with BED leadership.
10 
 
 
 
 Mission and values remain unchanged. 
 2030 vision updated to place renewable supply more prominently, though the underlying 
vision (a Net Zero Energy City displacing fossil fuel use in thermal and ground 
transportation sectors with 100% renewable electricity) remains the same. This change 
responds to commission feedback requesting clearer emphasis on continued renewable 
electricity procurement (e.g., recent hydro purchases). 
 
Structural changes addressed prior feedback that the strategic objectives mixed action items and 
objectives together. The document is now organized into strategic pillars, with focus areas, action 
items, and objectives nested beneath each. The content was preserved from the previous draft 
(reϐlecting BED's ongoing bottom-up process of gathering input from each organizational area) but 
edited for conciseness. The pillars largely mirror the prior draft's strategic objectives: engaging 
community, strength and reliability, people/process/technology, innovation toward net zero, and 
managing ϐinances/affordability. 
 
New content highlights include:  
 A new bullet on renewable supply and load management, emphasizing adequate renewable 
supply and prioritization of long-term, stably priced procurements. 
 Advancing battery storage and local renewable energy projects (e.g., the solar canopy 
proposal discussed this evening). 
 Finance/affordability section includes equity components, risk management, and 
budget/ϐinance elements. 
 Process improvement section includes implementing the ARC audit recommendations as 
the ϐirst listed objective for this ϐiscal year. 
 
Mr. Springer described this version as a "hybrid approach," with a possible more substantial 
overhaul next year, pending further internal socialization of the document. BED’s goal is to balance 
comprehensiveness with focus on key priorities. 
 
Commissioner Vota praised the iteration and collaborative process with Chair Kenney and 
encouraged continuing to push further next year, using the document to signal intent on more 
aspirational goals (noting the balance needed between aspirational and tangible/actionable 
content), including items related to McNeil. 
 
Commissioner Kenney praised the improved clarity of the document and recommended aligning the 
strategic direction process with the budgeting cycle. Commissioner Kenney also recommended 
continuing to shift toward objective-oriented language, with action items framed as deliverables 
supporting those objectives.
11 
 
 
 
Commissioner Kenney asked how progress on key results (e.g., those appearing in the ϐinance 
section) is tracked, both internally and with the commission. 
 
Mr. Springer noted that dashboard work can be tied back to strategic direction items and proposed 
that an FY28 revision could better align dashboard items with the strategic direction, potentially 
streamlining less-relevant dashboard metrics while elevating the most important ones. Mr. Springer 
conϐirmed that many items are currently tracked via the dashboard and the net zero energy 
roadmap work, with further decluttering possible going forward. 
 
Commissioner Bonn expressed support, noting the document looks strong and should help support 
the mission and staff. 
 
Commissioner Williams praised the document and highlighted the planned KPI/dashboard 
revisions as a key next step and agreed with Commissioner Kenney's recommendation to align the 
strategic direction process with the budgeting cycle so budget decisions can ϐlow from the 
completed strategic planning. 
 
Mr. Springer acknowledged contributions from Emily Stebbins-Wheelock, Munir Kasti, Paul 
Alexander, Mike Kanarick, and Dan Edson in developing the revised document, noting plans to 
socialize it more fully across the organization before the next version. 
 
Commissioner Vota made a motion that the commission approve the 2026-2027 Strategic Direction 
as presented at tonight’s meeting. Commissioner Dawson seconded the motion. Vote: 5 aye 0 nay.  
 
12. Commissioners’ Check-In 
No topics were discussed.  
 
Adjourn  
Commissioner Williams made a motion to adjourn; the motion was seconded by Commissioner 
Bonn. Vote: 5 ayes 0 nays. 
 
The meeting of the Burlington Electric Commission adjourned at 6:47 p.m. 
 
Microsoft Teams transcript used to draft minutes prepared by Katie Morris and edited by Emily 
Stebbins-Wheelock, CFO and Manager of Strategy & Innovation.
